web_evidence.title: Dear Edward sample
web_evidence.note: Penguin’s sustained 35-page sample narrates multiple characters and the post-crash timeline externally in third person, while entering their thoughts; no participating narrator frames the prose.

web_evidence.title: Ann Napolitano Writing Styles in Dear Edward
web_evidence.note: Its point-of-view analysis explicitly says both storylines use third person, with shifting character focus on the plane and Edward-focused narration in the other storyline.

web_evidence.title: Dear Edward Summary and Study Guide
web_evidence.note: Describes the two timelines as third-person omniscient prose exploring the experiences and emotions of multiple characters.

web_evidence.title: Dear Edward Literary Elements
web_evidence.note: Explicitly identifies the novel’s narrator and point of view as third person.

search_log: Searched “Dear Edward Ann Napolitano excerpt first chapter publisher” and found Penguin’s authorized 35-page sample.
Searched “Dear Edward Ann Napolitano point of view third person narrator” and opened BookRags, GradeSaver, and SuperSummary whole-book descriptions.

Searched “Dear Edward alternating timeline narration point of view”; sources describe two timelines and shifting focal characters, but consistently retain third person rather than alternating grammatical person.
Searched Penguin Random House for an excerpt; its product page confirmed the edition and publisher but supplied synopsis rather than diagnostic prose.
Searched exact quote strings including “Fatherhood is, for him, one jolt of terror after another” and matched the quote to its sustained third-person context in the Penguin sample.
Opened Ann Napolitano’s book-club Q&A; it corroborated the plane-chapter/Edward-chapter structure but did not explicitly identify narrative person.
person_note: The diagnostic event passages repeatedly render Edward and other characters externally as he or she while accessing their thoughts. Penguin’s authorized opening sample independently demonstrates sustained third-person narration across multiple focal characters and across both the flight and post-crash material. Whole-book study sources explicitly confirm that both timelines remain in third person. First- and second-person forms in the quote set occur in dialogue, epigraphs, or generic maxims; the letters mentioned by sources are embedded objects rather than a constitutive first-person narrative strand. The main limitation is that the authorized prose source covers only the opening, but the explicit whole-book sources and interior Goodreads passages remove meaningful uncertainty.
